items.title: Trees pull water up under tension that could split steel
items.claim: A 100-metre redwood lifts water from roots to crown without any pump. The xylem column is under NEGATIVE pressure (tension) of -1 to -2 megapascals — enough to cavitate steel cables. The water column holds because of cohesion between water molecules.

options.text: Evaporation at the leaf surface pulls on the continuous water column; cohesion (hydrogen bonds between water molecules) plus adhesion to xylem walls transmits the tension all the way to the roots — the cohesion-tension theory (Dixon & Joly, 1894)

items.reveal_title: The tallest pump that isn't a pump
items.reveal:
Atmospheric pressure can only lift water about 10 metres against a vacuum. So redwoods aren't being pushed from below — they are being PULLED from above.

Evaporation at leaf stomata creates a curved water meniscus. Surface tension at this meniscus reduces pressure in the underlying xylem to less than zero (real negative pressure, not just sub-atmospheric). Hydrogen bonds between water molecules keep the column intact under tension.

If the tension breaks, you get cavitation: a bubble forms and the column ruptures. Trees minimise this by having millions of redundant narrow xylem vessels.

The theoretical maximum height for a tree, set by cavitation risk and gravitational pull on the water, is about 130 metres. The tallest known tree, Hyperion (a coast redwood), is 115.7 metres — close to the physical limit.
items.why: Pumps push. Trees pull — and the pulling reaches pressures so negative they should rip the liquid apart. The molecular cohesion of water is one of biology's most exploited features.

items.title: Most adult humans can't digest milk — and that's normal
items.claim: Babies make lactase to digest lactose in milk. In most of the world's adults, lactase production switches off after weaning. Adult milk-drinkers — common in Europeans and some African and Middle Eastern populations — carry a recently evolved mutation.

options.text: Adult lactose intolerance is ancestral; lactase persistence is a derived trait that arose in populations that domesticated dairy animals in the last 10,000 years

items.reveal:
Roughly 65 percent of adult humans globally show reduced lactase production after weaning. Lactase persistence is most common in northern Europeans (around 90 percent), some West African pastoralist groups, and some Middle Eastern populations.

Different regulatory mutations independently produced this trait in different lineages — convergent evolution. The European variant (a single nucleotide change near the LCT gene, called T-13910) is dated to about 5,000 to 10,000 years ago, coinciding with cattle domestication.

Dairy farming and lactase persistence appear to have co-evolved: ancient DNA shows farmers drank milk before persistence was common, suggesting cultural use (fermented dairy, lower lactose) preceded biological adaptation. As populations relied more on milk, the persistence allele was strongly selected.
items.why: European diets are taken as a baseline; lactose intolerance is treated as a disorder. Globally, lactose intolerance IS the baseline — milk drinking adults are the rare ones.

items.title: Reintroducing wolves changed the course of rivers in Yellowstone
items.claim: Grey wolves were exterminated from Yellowstone by 1926. In 1995, 14 wolves were reintroduced. Within 20 years, elk populations dropped, willows and aspen regrew along riverbanks, beaver populations rose, and river channels narrowed.

options.text: A trophic cascade: wolves reduce elk numbers and (especially) keep them moving, releasing browse pressure on streamside trees, which stabilise banks. The effect propagates through multiple trophic levels
Wolves drink large amounts of river water
It's coincidence — climate change did it

items.reveal:
The Yellowstone story is the textbook trophic cascade. Wolves don't only kill elk; they shift elk behaviour — herds avoid areas where they can't see predators coming, like valley bottoms with dense vegetation.

Released from constant browsing, willows and aspens regrow. Beavers, which need willows, return — by 2014, beaver colonies had increased from 1 to 9. Beaver dams trap sediment, raise water tables, create wetlands.

The full claim ('wolves changed the rivers') is contested. William Ripple and Robert Beschta documented the vegetation rebound; Arthur Middleton and others argue confounding factors (climate, bear predation, elk hunting outside the park) explain much of it.

What is uncontroversial: keystone species have effects on ecosystems vastly out of proportion to their biomass. Sea otters and kelp forests, starfish and intertidal communities, sharks and seagrass — similar cascades documented worldwide.

Keystone species concept: Robert Paine (1969), who removed starfish from a Pacific Northwest tide pool and watched it collapse to a mussel monoculture.
items.why: Ecosystems are imagined as bottom-up: plants determine herbivores determine carnivores. Top predators flip the picture — top-down control is real, and big effects can come from species with little biomass.
